summary: This memo defines MIB objects for managing the bridge Network Control Protocol on interfaces that use the Point-to-Point Protocol family. It is historic.

eli5.summary: PPP connects two computers over a line. This paper lists what a network manager can check about the part that joins two networks together. It is historic.

questions: what is the ppp bridge mib
subtitle: Managing bridging between networks over Point-to-Point Protocol links

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standard way to monitor and manage the bridge control protocol for PPP links, which allow connecting two local area networks across a serial connection.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1474 defines SNMP MIB objects for the Bridge Network Control Protocol of PPP, organized into operational status objects and configuration parameters, including compression and LAN identification options.
tldr.outcome: This specification became historic as PPP usage declined and higher-speed technologies replaced serial links as the primary means for connecting networks.

today: RFC 1474 is Historic. While PPP remains in use for some applications, the primary role of bridging over serial lines has been replaced by modern networking technologies. PPP itself is rarely used for WAN connectivity in modern networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1474 defines a set of management objects (MIB) for controlling and monitoring the Bridge Network Control Protocol used on Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) interfaces. PPP is a protocol for sending data over serial links between two devices.

The RFC allows network administrators to use SNMP to check the status of bridge operations, configure compression settings, and manage the LAN identification options used when bridging two networks over a PPP connection. All management objects defined in this RFC are mandatory for implementations of PPP that support bridging.
sections.eli5: This describes what a network manager can watch about bridging (connecting two networks) over a simple point-to-point serial link.

sections.title: PPP and Network Control Protocols
sections.content:
PPP is actually a family of protocols working together. The Link Control Protocol (LCP) establishes and controls the connection itself. Above that, Network Protocols handle the actual data traffic (such as Bridging or IP protocols). For each network protocol, there is a corresponding Network Control Protocol (NCP) that manages its operation.

RFC 1474 specifies management objects for the Bridge NCP, which is the control protocol for bridging (RFC 1220). This allows two local area networks connected by a PPP link to appear as a single network, with bridge learning and frame forwarding happening across the serial link.
sections.eli5: PPP has control protocols that manage how different types of network traffic work over the serial link. This RFC covers the control protocol for bridging.

sections.title: Operational and Configuration Objects
sections.content:
RFC 1474 defines two tables of management objects. The PPP Bridge Table contains operational status information: whether the bridge protocol has opened (negotiation complete) and two optional compression settings negotiated between the local and remote systems.

The PPP Bridge Configuration Table contains configuration parameters that administrators can set: the desired administrative status (open or close), whether to enable Tinygram Compression (a technique to save bandwidth by combining small packets), and LAN identification settings. Both tables are indexed by interface, allowing a system with multiple PPP links to manage each bridge independently.
sections.eli5: One table shows what is currently happening (open or closed), and another table shows settings an administrator can change.

sections.title: Compression and LAN Identification
sections.content:
Tinygram Compression reduces bandwidth on the serial link by combining multiple small packets into a single transmission. RFC 1474 tracks whether Tinygram Compression is enabled in each direction of the link: from local to remote, and from remote to local. This allows asymmetric configuration if needed.

The LAN Identification Option allows the inclusion of a field that identifies which source LAN a bridged frame came from. This is tracked separately for each direction. The RFC notes that these values are only meaningful after the bridge protocol has reached the open state, indicated by the operational status object.
sections.eli5: The manager can see if compression is being used and whether the systems are adding a label showing which network the traffic came from.

sections.title: Administrative Control
sections.content:
The configuration table includes an administrative status object that allows operators to request the bridge protocol to open or close. When set to open, it injects an open event into the bridge protocol's state machine; when set to close, it injects a close event. This allows operators to start, stop, or restart bridging without reloading software.

RFC 1474 explicitly states that the protocol negotiation values (compression and LAN ID settings) are only meaningful after negotiation completes and the link reaches the open state. Before that, the values are implementation-dependent and should not be interpreted.
sections.eli5: An administrator can command the bridge to open or close the connection, and can see the settings that were negotiated.
